10043-klondyke-nuggets-a-brief-descripti:
Joseph Ladue, founder of Dawson City in the Northwest Territories, wrote this brief description of the great gold regions in September 1897. Gold fever was sweeping the world, and Ladue, an explorer, miner, and prospector, knew the Klondyke from personal residence and practical experience.

His book explains the country, the diggings, and the routes, for readers tempted to join the rush. Written by a man who had just returned for a temporary stay, it carries the authority of firsthand knowledge. It remains a vivid source on the Klondike gold rush at the moment it broke.
10477-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-01:
John Lord published this first volume of Beacon Lights of History, on the old pagan civilizations, in a new edition that rearranged his lectures. Lord began with classic antiquity, then returned to remoter times, reaching back to Assyria and Egypt, before moving to Jewish heroes and on to modern days. His wife Mary Porter Lord encouraged his long labors.

The volume treats pagan peoples thousands of years before the Hebrews, through great men and movements rather than dry dates. Later volumes will follow Rome, the Middle Ages, and modern Europe. Readers get a readable, old-style history by biography, full of moral lessons and vivid scenes.
11861-radio-boys-cronies-or-bill-brown-s:
Wayne Whipple's boys' novel follows Bill Brown, a quick-witted teenager who walks with a crutch, and his athletic friend Gus Grier of Fairview. The two hurry to hear a radio talk. Bill's gift for copying Morse code soon puts him at the center of the town's new wireless excitement.

Chapters mix schoolboy humor with early radio detail: operators testing speed, friends crowding around a set, and Bill retelling a talk he heard over the air. Written when broadcasting was still a novelty, the story treats radio as both a hobby and a test of character, rewarding patience, accuracy, and loyalty between friends.
12249-bart-ridgeley-a-story-of-northern-:
A. G. Riddle published Bart Ridgeley in 1873, a story of northern Ohio in the years before and during the Civil War. Riddle, an Ohio lawyer and judge, sets the novel among farms, villages, and county courts.

Chapters follow Bart from failure and the blue chamber through Newbury, the post office, and Mrs. Markham views, to logic of the gods, a ramble in the woods, and a darkened soul. Later chapters bring Blackstone, the young idea shooting, snow parties, waltzes, and sugar making. A mid-book thread follows a lost girl in fallen timber, seeking a passage through the woods. The novel mixes romance with law and politics, showing Ohio life in transition.
12853-the-wearing-of-the-green-or-the-pr:
Published in Dublin in 1868, this pamphlet-book tells of the funeral procession prosecuted after the Manchester executions of November 23, 1867. News of the hanging of three Irishmen fell on Ireland, the author says, with stupor and amazement, since few had believed England would carry out the sentence. Grief turned swiftly to public protest.

Much of the book reports the court fight that followed, with witnesses summoned, magistrates questioned, and claims of unfair dealing aired in detail. Sir John Gray and other public men appear among the witnesses. The work stands as a partisan, on-the-spot record of Irish feeling in a bitter year.
14909-elsie-s-new-relations-what-they-di:
Martha Finley's Elsie's New Relations, a sequel to Grandmother Elsie, follows what new relations did and how they fared at Ion, published by Burt in 1911. Late October finds the Dinsmores, Travillas and Raymonds in two cottages, after three or four months by the sea.

Woods behind the cottages glow scarlet, crimson and gold, sea air delights, summer visitors have fled and the beach lies almost deserted as Edward and his child wife wander slowly along it. Verses from Mrs. Hemans open the book, praising kind looks and words showered like dew. Finley keeps her family circle at the centre, with faith, affection and seaside calm.
15713-what-philately-teaches-a-lecture-d:
John N. Luff delivered this lecture on what philately teaches before the section on philately of the Brooklyn Institute of Arts and Sciences on February 24, 1899. A third edition appeared in New York in 1915. Luff hopes to interest non-collectors, and to show the instructive things learned by following this fascinating pursuit, apologizing for any dryness to seasoned philatelists.

Stamp collecting, Luff argues, has become more than an amusement for children. It affords instruction and mental relaxation to older, more serious minds. Every stamp album and catalogue, he says, should bear the old Latin motto Te doces, thou teachest. Stamps teach geography, history, art, printing, and politics, country by country, reign by reign. The lecture defends a hobby as a liberal education in miniature, open to anyone with an album and curiosity.
15870-of-genius-in-the-occasional-paper-:
An Augustan Reprint Society booklet pairing two early eighteenth-century texts on genius. Series Four, number two, issued in March 1949 at one dollar, with an introduction by Gretchen Graf Pahl. The first text, Of Genius, appeared anonymously in The Occasional Paper in 1719. The second is Aaron Hill's preface to The Creation of 1720.

Together the pieces show Augustan writers asking what genius is: gift, fire, or learned skill. Hill's preface defends a sacred poem in heroic terms. Pahl's introduction sets both texts in their literary moment. The booklet suits students of criticism: short, sharp, and rooted in the age when genius became a modern word.
20850-prince-prigio:
A queen who scorns fairies rules the court where Prince Prigio grows up. She swears fairies never lived, though the royal family's own history brims with them. Andrew Lang sets that comic clash at the heart of his fairy tale.

Prigio, too clever for his own good, gets gifts he never asked for. Magic caps, swords, and carpets tumble him into droll scrapes. Lang retold old tales for a living, and here he invents with glee. Prince Prigio stays among his best-loved tales, sly and swift, with a hero who must learn that brains alone cannot win a heart.
21381-stories-of-ohio:
William Dean Howells, Ohio's most famous novelist, wrote these stories in 1897 to give readers the history of his home state in outline. He opens with the Ice Folk and the Earth Folk, when glaciers pushed down from the north and covered much of the earth. Ohio's story runs from the ice to the Civil War generation.

Chapters follow Ohio as part of France, then English. The forty years' war for the West comes next, then the captivities of James Smith, Boone, and Kenton. The torture of Colonel Crawford and the state's wickedest deed get their due. Howells drew on Parkman, Henry Howe's collections, and Roosevelt's Winning of the West, and says his purpose of truth never failed.
21770-the-author-of-beltraffio:
A young American admirer keeps a letter of introduction in his pocket for three weeks in this Henry James tale of 1885. He is too shy to use it. The author he longs to meet is Mark Ambient, whose novel Beltraffio has caused a stir, even a scandal. James calls the book the most complete statement yet of the gospel of art.

The narrator has read Beltraffio five times and holds his visit back like a trump card. When the meeting comes, the great man's home life proves stranger than his fame. James studies the gap between the public artist and the private man. It is one of his sharp early tales of art, worship, and disillusion.
21859-historical-sketches-volume-i-of-3-:
Essays on Turks, Cicero, Apollonius, and the early Church fill this first volume of John Henry Newman's Historical Sketches, reprinted here in 1908. Newman gathers pieces written across his career, one of them first framed when he was still an Anglican controversialist. His dedication to Bishop Moriarty of Kerry explains the oddity with grace. He says he could not ask a Catholic bishop's formal leave, yet inscribes the book to him anyway.

The Turks are studied in their long relation to Europe. Cicero gets a portrait as orator and statesman. Apollonius of Tyana and primitive Christianity bring the volume into the early Church. Newman writes history as a man of faith and letters, with long, balanced sentences and deep learning worn lightly.
22631-an-account-of-timbuctoo-and-housa-:
An Account of Timbuctoo and Housa Territories in the Interior of Africa is a travel narrative of the western Sudan, drawn from the life of a Moroccan merchant and pilgrim. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Few Europeans had seen Timbuktu, and accounts from Muslim travelers carried rare weight.

The sample follows its subject at twenty-seven, leaving Tetuan with a caravan for Egypt on pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina. He returned to trade from his native town, then sailed for Hamburg to buy linens and goods his commerce needed. Only after such a life did his knowledge of the interior take shape. The account preserves routes, peoples, and markets of Hausaland and Timbuktu as a working trader knew them.
2270-shakespeare-s-first-folio:
Published in 1623 by Shakespeare's fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell, the First Folio gathered thirty-six plays into one great book. Without it, eighteen plays, including Macbeth, Twelfth Night, and Julius Caesar, might have vanished entirely. This hosted text preserves the Folio's wording, with its old spellings and printers' quirks intact.

The volume opens with praise from Ben Jonson and a portrait of the playwright, then moves through comedies, histories, and tragedies in its original order. For students of Shakespeare, the Folio is the foundation text, closest to the playing company's own scripts. Reading it is like entering the playhouse of Shakespeare's own age.
2448-henry-ossian-flipper-the-colored-ca:
Henry Ossian Flipper, the first Black graduate of West Point, tells his own story in this autobiography. The Colored Cadet at West Point follows Flipper from enslavement in Georgia through the Academy's isolation and prejudice to his commission in 1877. His account is dignified, detailed, and restrained.

The memoir matters as a firsthand record of a pioneer who broke a color line and later faced a court-martial and dismissal. Flipper's story illuminates both the Army and the nation after Reconstruction. Readers of American history will find an essential voice. Flipper later worked as a mining engineer in the American West.
3145-the-author-of-beltraffio:
Henry James builds this novella around a young admirer and the famous author he longs to meet. The narrator keeps his letter of introduction in his pocket-book for three weeks. He feels nervous and timid, conscious of youth and ignorance, and sure the great man is tormented by strangers. That delay sets the story's uneasy tone.

When the meeting comes, admiration meets a household at odds over art itself. James studies the cost of a literary life: a wife who fears her husband's books, a child caught between parents, and a visitor who must choose what loyalty means. The tale is short, tense, and quietly devastating about the price of genius.
4639-california-romantic-and-resourceful:
John F. Davis wrote California Romantic and Resourceful as a plea for the collection, preservation, and diffusion of information relating to Pacific Coast history. He opens with David Starr Jordan's line that the Californian loves his state because his state loves him, with a fierce affection that surprises strangers. Davis looks forward to future ages and populations, to cities gemming the sea's borders, and to all peoples and tongues meeting on that shore.

As institutions are transmitted, he says, so blood and names pass to future generations, toward a more perfect civilisation, firmer faith, and more reverent worship. Some thoughtful man of letters yet to come, he hopes, may bring light to the history of that shore and day. Readers get a short, earnest California address, useful for local history, and for the early case that a young state's records deserve careful keeping.
4715-an-african-millionaire-episodes-in-:
Grant Allen tells An African Millionaire in twelve episodes from the life of the illustrious Colonel Clay. Its narrator, Seymour Wilbraham Wentworth, is brother-in-law and secretary to Sir Charles Vandrift, a South African millionaire and famous financier. Years earlier, when Charlie Vandrift was a small lawyer in Cape Town, Wentworth married his sister, and later joined him when the Vandrift farm near Kimberley grew into the Cloetedorp Golcondas.

Wentworth insists no common sharper can take Vandrift in, a sharp, successful business genius of middle height and firm mouth. Only one rogue ever imposed on him, a man police said could have fooled Vidocq, Houdin, and Cagliostro together. Episodes follow a Mexican seer, diamond links, an old master, a Tyrolean castle, a drawn game, a German professor, and more. Readers get a witty swindler tale, with Clay outwitting wealth in disguise after disguise.
500-the-adventures-of-pinocchio:
Carlo Collodi, writing as C. Collodi, tells of a wooden puppet who longs to become a real boy in this Italian classic, here in Carol Della Chiesa's translation. A talking log becomes Pinocchio in Geppetto's shop, then runs off into lies, school truancy, and scrapes with a fox, a cat, and a whale.

Each misdeed lengthens his nose or lands him in deeper trouble, until love and hard work teach him care for others. Collodi writes with brisk humor and sharp morals, never softening the knocks. The book endures worldwide as a tale of how a foolish puppet learns, at last, to be human.
5192-on-a-dynamical-top-for-exhibiting-t:
James Clerk Maxwell's paper, read to the Royal Society of Edinburgh on April 20, 1857, explains how a spinning top can show the motion of a rigid body about a fixed point. Maxwell takes the familiar toy as a model for the mathematics of rotation, and draws out what the top's behaviour suggests about the motion of the earth itself.

The paper belongs to Maxwell's early work in mathematical physics, written before his famous equations on electricity and magnetism. Readers with some physics will find a clear, elegant example of Victorian science. A child's toy becomes a tool for thinking about planets and the spinning earth.
5219-the-satyricon-volume-02-dinner-of-t:
This second volume of Petronius's Satyricon, in W. C. Firebaugh's complete translation, contains the famous Dinner of Trimalchio. Encolpius and his companions attend a feast given by Trimalchio, a freedman grown enormously rich, whose vulgar display, endless courses, and anxious boasts provide the comedy.

The dinner episode, running from chapter twenty-seven onward, is the best known part of the surviving Satyricon, and it gives a vivid picture of Roman luxury and social climbing. Readers get satire at its sharpest, as Petronius lets his host talk himself into absurdity course by course.
5227-sant-ilario:
F. Marion Crawford's Sant' Ilario is the second part of Saracinesca, dedicated to the author's wife. It opens two years into the service of Anastase Gouache, a painter turned Zouave, whose weather-browned skin. His compact frame hardened as well, showing what soldiering had made of a delicate artist. It follows the Roman families whose fortunes intertwine with his.

Crawford sets love, honour, and family pride against the Rome of his day, with the pacing of a popular romance. Readers who enjoy nineteenth-century Italian novels will find here a sequel that stands on its own as a story of art, war, and aristocratic life.
6433-on-the-trail-of-pontiac-or-the-pion:
Edward Stratemeyer, in the fourth volume of his Colonial Series, sends pioneer boys of the Ohio on the trail of Pontiac, as a complete story in itself. Two wild turkeys and seven rabbits make a haul, Henry Morris says, though he wanted a deer. Dave Morris agrees that deer are scarcer than before the war, when they came within a hundred yards of the house.

Game should be plentiful, Dave argues, since little hunting happened near home during the war, when most able men went to the front. Others stayed, afraid of pay or of French and Indians knocking them over. A later scene leaves a boy buried in dirt, clearing hands and body in pitch dark rain, muttering he is in a pickle truly. Stratemeyer writes frontier boys' adventure with hunting, hardship, and history close at hand.
8156-twilight-and-dawn-or-simple-talks-o:
Caroline Pridham, Mrs L. G. Wait, wrote these simple talks on the six days of creation for young readers, under the title Twilight and Dawn. Her contents move from God's book and in the beginning, through creation, ruin, and darkness, to the first day of light, the second day's ocean of air. The third day's waters, earth, and green plants, the fourth day's sun, moon, and stars, the fifth day's moving creatures and fowl, and the sixth day's animals and man. A story of a deaf boy who heard the sun proclaim God's glory is included.

Pridham writes plainly, tying each day's work to nature a child can see, and to the stone book of geology. The talks suit family reading and Sunday schools of their era. As a Victorian children's book on Genesis, it shows how faith and natural history were once taught together, simply and reverently.
8301-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-01-gene:
Genesis opens the Douay-Rheims Bible, the English Catholic translation made from the Latin Vulgate and revised by Bishop Richard Challoner in the mid-1700s. It begins with the creation of heaven and earth, the garden, the fall, and the flood, then follows the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and closes with Joseph in Egypt. The whole sweep runs from the first days to a family settled in a foreign land.

Challoner's wording keeps the older Catholic phrasing, with notes drawn from the Vulgate tradition. Genesis gives readers the founding stories of Israel's faith: covenant promises, sibling rivalry, exile, and return. As the first book of this historic translation, it sets the tone for all that follows.
8304-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-04-numb:
Numbers counts Israel in the desert, and the counting frames a story of wandering, complaint, and slow growth. The Douay-Rheims book, in Challoner's revision, follows the tribes from Sinai toward the promised land. Censuses, camp orders, and laws for priests sit beside spies who fear giants, rebels swallowed by the earth, and a bronze serpent lifted to heal snakebite.

Forty years pass in these pages, and a whole generation dies in the wilderness while a new one grows up to enter. Moses himself, striking a rock in anger, is barred from the land he sought. Numbers is the least tidy book of the law, mixing lists and drama, and it shows a people learning, painfully, to trust.
8309-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-09-1-ki:
Samuel stands at the hinge of Israel's story in this book, which the Douay-Rheims tradition numbers as 1 Kings. It opens with Hannah's prayer for a child, follows Samuel as prophet and judge, and tells how the people demanded a king. Saul rises, fails, and falls, while David, the shepherd boy who slew Goliath, waits in the wings.

The narrative runs from a childless woman's vow to a kingdom torn by war, with David's friendship with Jonathan and his flight from Saul at its heart. Challoner's revision keeps the old Catholic names and wording from the Latin Vulgate. Readers who know this history as 1 Samuel will find the same story under the Douay numbering.
8310-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-10-2-ki:
David's reign, in all its triumph and trouble, fills this book, numbered 2 Kings in the Douay-Rheims Bible. It opens with news of Saul's death and follows David's rise in Hebron and Jerusalem. It tells of the ark's arrival, the promise of a lasting house, and then the king's great failures: adultery with Bethsabee, murder by proxy, and rebellion by his own son Absalom.

The book closes with an old king, a census punished by plague, and a threshing floor bought for an altar. Readers who know the story as 2 Samuel will recognize every scene under Douay numbering. Challoner's Vulgate-based text gives it in the older Catholic spelling, Bethsabee for Bathsheba, and a grave, measured tone.
8311-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-11-3-ki:
Solomon's glory and the kingdom's split fill this book, counted as 3 Kings in the Douay-Rheims numbering. David dies, Solomon asks for wisdom, and the temple rises in Jerusalem in splendor. Then the kingdom breaks: ten tribes follow Jeroboam north, while Judah stays loyal to David's line in the south. Prophets confront kings, and Elijah's contest on Mount Carmel stands at the center.

Challoner's text, revised from the Latin Vulgate in the mid-1700s, keeps the older Catholic naming, so readers used to modern Bibles will know this book as 1 Kings. Its story moves from gold and wisdom to idols, drought, and civil war, a long fall told with a chronicler's patience.
8312-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-12-4-ki:
Two kingdoms slide toward ruin in this book, counted as 4 Kings in the Douay-Rheims Bible. Elijah confronts Ahab and Jezabel, Elisha inherits his mantle and works wonders, and then the northern kingdom falls to Assyria, its people scattered. Judah holds on longer, through good kings like Ezechias and the boy king Josias, who finds the book of the law in the temple.

The end comes with Babylon: Jerusalem besieged, the temple burned, and the people carried off. A final note of mercy, the captive king eating at a foreign table, closes the history. Readers used to modern Bibles know this book as 2 Kings, told here in Challoner's older Catholic English from the Vulgate.
8338-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-38-mich:
Micheas is the Douay-Rheims name for Micah, a prophet of the countryside who preached against Jerusalem's rulers. He denounces judges who take bribes, prophets who bless for pay, and landlords who seize fields, and he warns that the city will be plowed like a field. Yet the book also holds one of the Bible's most quoted lines: do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with God.

A promise of a ruler from Bethlehem, small among Judah's towns, closes the prophetic hope, and Christians read it as pointing to Jesus. Challoner's revision from the Vulgate keeps the older spelling and the prophet's blunt, rural voice. Micheas is short, fierce, and practical, a book about what God actually wants from his people.
8340-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-40-haba:
Habacuc is the Douay-Rheims name for Habakkuk, a prophet who argued with God rather than merely speaking for him. He asks why the wicked prosper and why God would use a crueler nation, Babylon, to punish Judah. God's answers do not explain everything, but they promise that the just shall live by faith, and that violence will answer for itself.

The book closes with a hymn of trust, praising God though fig trees fail and fields yield no food. Challoner's Vulgate-based text gives the short book in older Catholic English. Readers who find easy answers hollow return to Habacuc, because it lets doubt speak first and still ends in stubborn faith.
8347-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-47-matt:
Matthew's Gospel opens the New Testament in the Douay-Rheims Bible, tracing Jesus back to Abraham and David. It tells of wise men from the east, the Sermon on the Mount, parables of the kingdom, and clashes with scribes and Pharisees, building to the crucifixion and the empty tomb. The closing commission sends the disciples to all nations.

Challoner's revision from the Vulgate keeps the older Catholic wording, with notes that shaped English Catholic reading for generations. Matthew is the most orderly Gospel, arranged in five great teaching blocks, and the most Jewish in flavor, quoting the prophets at every turn. For readers new to the Gospels, it offers the fullest teaching of Jesus in one place.
8365-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-65-hebr:
Hebrews argues, like a sermon, that Jesus surpasses all that came before: angels, Moses, and the high priests of the old covenant. Its unknown author builds the case from Scripture, showing a single sacrifice replacing repeated temple offerings, and a high priest who understands weakness because he shared it. The Douay-Rheims text gives the argument in Challoner's formal, Vulgate-based English.

The famous roll of faith then marches from Abel to the prophets, praising those who trusted without seeing. It closes with calls to endure, to honor marriage, and to care for strangers. Hebrews rewards slow reading, dense and poetic, and it has shaped Christian ideas of priesthood and sacrifice more than any other New Testament book.
8367-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-67-1-pe:
Christians scattered across Asia Minor, facing suspicion and insult, receive this letter in Peter's name. It calls them a chosen generation and a royal priesthood, strangers in a world that watches them, and urges them to live so well that accusers find nothing true to charge. Advice for households, respect for rulers, and patience under unjust suffering follow.

The letter's image of the devil prowling like a roaring lion warns readers to stay sober and watchful. In Challoner's Douay-Rheims wording, the counsel keeps its older Catholic tone. For believers under pressure, 1 Peter offers dignity rather than escape: suffering, borne without returning evil, is part of following Christ.
8678-the-english-governess-at-the-siames:
Anna Harriette Leonowens recalls six years as governess in the royal palace at Bangkok, in the court of the King of Siam. Her memoir, illustrated from photographs given by the king himself, describes palace life from inside: its ceremonies, its women and children, its politics, and the daily work of teaching royal pupils. Leonowens dedicates the book to a friend who urged her to try her fortunes in a new country.

The recollections mix wonder, humour, and criticism, as an English widow navigates a court run by rules very different from her own. Her account later inspired plays and films, though historians now read it with care, since some details have been questioned. As a Victorian travel memoir it remains gripping, and as a source on Siam it offers a rare, close view of a palace few outsiders ever entered.
9574-poems-of-nature-poems-subjective-an:
Volume two of Whittier's complete works gathers three groups of his verse in one book: Poems of Nature, Poems Subjective and Reminiscent, and Religious Poems. Nature poems run from The Frost Spirit and Hampton Beach to mountain views and autumn walks. Memory poems include The Barefoot Boy, My Psalm, and Snow-Bound. Religious verse spans The Star of Bethlehem, The Crucifixion, and hymns of trust.

Taken whole, the volume shows Whittier's full range: woods and shores, home and youth, prayer and faith. His voice stays plain, earnest, and Quaker-true through all three modes. A reader gets the core of Whittier's lyric art in a single volume, and a fine guide to why he long stood among America's beloved poets.
an-african-millionaire-episodes-in-the-l:
Grant Allen's An African Millionaire tells episodes in the life of the illustrious Colonel Clay. Colonel Clay is a master swindler whose quarry is Sir Charles Vandrift. Vandrift, a South African diamond millionaire, is robbed again and again. His secretary and brother-in-law narrates each defeat with rueful admiration.

The Episode of the Mexican Seer opens the campaign of disguise. Diamond links, a forged old master, and a Tyrolean episode follow in the contents. Clay changes face, voice, and trade faster than detectives can follow. Allen, a science writer turned novelist, makes crime a duel of wits. Each story asks how the trick was done this time. The book is a rogue's gallery in reverse: the criminal is the hero, and the millionaire the comic victim.
california-romantic-and-resourceful-a-pl:
John F. Davis wrote California Romantic and Resourceful as a plea for Pacific Coast history. Davis, a San Francisco lawyer, grew the book from two addresses. One marked Admission Day at Colton Hall in Monterey in 1908. The other spoke to the Commonwealth Club in 1913, with statistics revised to that year's end.

His argument is simple: Californians must collect, preserve, and spread their own records before they vanish. He praises new works on San Francisco's beginnings and a university fellowship in Pacific Coast history. The love story of Concha Argüello, the presidio girl who waited for her Russian lover, illustrates the romance he means. Illustrations show missions, Sutter's Mill, and old Monterey. Davis writes as a booster with a historian's conscience, urging pride to fund archives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-and-dio:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Bobbio treats both the abbey and the diocese suffragan to Genoa, coterminous with the civil district of Bobbio in the province of Pavia. Suppressed from 1803 to 1817 and annexed in turn to Alessandria and Casale, the diocese was re-established by Pius the Seventh in 1818.

Bobbio owes its origin to the monastery founded by the Irish saint Columban in 614, after Lombard invaders had swept northern Italy. Under Bishop Antonio Gianelli a congregation of Oblates of St. Alphonsus Liguori arose in 1839, hearing confessions in prisons and hospitals and spreading good literature, while the Gianelliane sisters served beside them. The entry joins diocesan history to the abbey's great missionary past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ajaccio:
Ajaccio, Adjacensis, comprises the island of Corsica. Formerly a suffragan of Pisa, since the French Concordat it has been Aix's suffragan. History's first known bishop was Evander, who assisted at Rome's council in 313. Before the Revolution Corsica held five other dioceses. Accia had been vacant since 1563. Aleria's bishop resided at Corte, Sagone's at Calvi, and Mariana's at Bastia. Nebbio was the fifth.

Pius X, appointing Desanti bishop in 1906, reserved the right to redraw diocesan limits, by which Bastia might be restored. Legend says bishops banished from Africa in 484 built Ajaccio's primitive cathedral with their own hands. The present late-sixteenth-century cathedral owes its building to Gregory XIII, who as Ugo Buoncompagni had served at Ajaccio as papal legate. Greek-rite services continue at Cargese, founded in 1676 by descendants of Stephen Comnenus, expelled from the Peloponnesus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessio:
Alessio, also called Lissus, is a diocese in European Turkey, suffragan of Scutari since 1886. It is one of the chief seaports of Albania, favourably placed near the mouth of the Drin. It once had five churches, and its cathedral, dedicated to St. Nicholas, once held the remains of the patriot George Castriota, known as Skanderbeg. On rocky hills across the Drin stand the church and convent of St. Anthony of Padua.

Within the diocese lies the quasi-episcopal abbey of St. Alexander of Orosci, an abbey exempt from any bishop's jurisdiction. The entry's sources include Farlati's Illyricum Sacrum, Gams's series of bishops, and Hecquard's Upper Albania, works that trace the diocese through centuries of change on Albania's coast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexis-franco:
Alexis-François Rio was a French writer on art, born on the Island of Arz in Morbihan in May 1797 and dead in June 1874. Educated at Vannes, where he first taught, he went to Paris hoping for a chair of history and was disappointed. His championship of Greek liberty drew the government's notice, which named him censor of the press, and he refused the post.

A Foreign Ministry post under minister de La Ferronays let Rio become, in Montalembert's phrase, for Christian art what Winckelmann had been to ancient art. He spent 1830 to 1860 travelling in Italy, Germany, and England. At Munich he met the spokesmen of contemporary Catholicism and learned the aesthetic ideal from Schelling. His Christian Art, begun in 1835, failed in France though welcomed in Germany and Italy. After years among England's Pre-Raphaelites and fresh tours of Europe's galleries, he published his studies in four volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Vexio, in Sweden, covered Kronoberg and the hundreds of Ostra, Westra, Ostbo, and Westbo in Jonkoping. John Sigfrid, an Englishman from Northumbria and court bishop to King Olaf Tryggvasson, left Norway for Sweden in 1002 and worked six years in Westergotland. About 1008 he reached Vexio, preached with success to Varend's heathens, built a wooden church there, and stayed until his death about 1030.

In 1158 Adrian IV canonized him, and his shrine graced the Cathedral of Saint John the Baptist and Saint Sigfrid until the Reformation. He left no immediate successors, and in 1126 King Sigurd Jorsalafarer of Norway led a crusade into Smaaland to Christianize its people. Varend belonged to Skara until 1100, then to Linkoping, until Vexio was re-erected about 1150. Stenar, first bishop, appears in letters from 1183, quarrelled with Linkoping over frontiers in 1191. John Ehrengisleson followed in 1193. A life of Saint Sigfrid was written in 1205.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-del-ve:
Andrea del Verrocchio was born at Florence in 1435 and died at Venice in 1488. Born Andrea di Michele di Francesco de' Cioni, he took the name of his master, the goldsmith Giuliano Verrocchio. Some say he frequented Donatello's and Baldovinetti's studios, but goldsmith training marks his work, above all in delicate chasing, seen in the Colleoni horse and harness.

He excelled in children and womanly grace. He never married, living in his sister's household. Favoured by Lorenzo de' Medici, he was reputed the greatest artist of his time, yet seems never to have known fortune's favours, though his art shines with smiling beauty. Painter and sculptor, he worked as a sculptor: the Medici tomb at San Lorenzo and his bronze David at the Bargello. His Baptism of 1470 broke with the fresco school. Vasari called his manner hard and crude and claimed Leonardo painted the angel guarding Christ's garments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-pallad:
Andrea Palladio, an Italian architect, was born at Vicenza in 1508 and died at Venice in 1580. Tradition makes him a poor carpenter's son, without a surname, until the poet Gian Giorgio Trissino, his patron, gave him the name Palladio, for Pallas, Greek goddess of wisdom. After a brief sculptor's apprenticeship he travelled, studying classical remains and seeking their principles with Vitruvius as guide.

His earliest known building is the Palazzo Godi at Lonedo, from 1540. Work on rebuilding his native town's basilica began in 1549, and its colonnades remain his most famous work. His triumphal arch at Vicenza still ranks as the best modern imitation of a Roman arch. Proportion, refinement, and invention mark his Vicenza palaces. He designed many villas, though few were finished. His writings spread his influence across Europe, with Inigo Jones as English editor, and American Georgian architecture descends from him. His manner is now called Palladian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-bosio:
Antonio Bosio, born in Malta about 1576 and dead in 1629, gave up law at eighteen to map the underground burial places of early Christians in Rome. A chance find on the Via Salaria in 1578 had stirred brief interest, yet almost no one pursued it further. Bosio made the work systematic, and the article credits him as the founder of Christian archaeology, the study of early Christian remains and sites.

He read widely before he dug, turning to acts of martyrs, council records, and Greek and Latin church fathers for clues to lost sites. That book learning guided his search through the catacombs, the tunnel burial grounds beneath Rome. Readers who want the birth of a field will find here a life spent joining texts to tunnels, so that scattered graves became a mapped record of the early church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnolfo-di-ca:
Arnolfo di Cambio, sometimes called di Lapo, principal master of Italian Gothic, was born at Florence about 1232. He died there in his seventy-first year, probably in 1300, during Dante's brief power. Who Arnolfo was is scarcely known, though few architects left greater works. Baldinucci, Cicognara, and Gaye say his father Cambio came from Colle in the Val d'Elsa. Arnolfo first appears among workmen on the Siena cathedral pulpit as pupil or journeyman of Nicola Pisano.

With him worked a certain Lapo, called by Vasari his father, by others his instructor, but very likely only a fellow workman. The same band under Nicola worked at Pisa, Perugia, Cortona, Orvieto, and Rome. Arnolfo had reached thirty when his father died, already of high repute, having learnt from his father whatever that master knew. The entry follows a Gothic builder from workshop hand to master of Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew-o:
Bartholomew of San Concordio was a canonist and man of letters, born near Pisa about 1260, who died at Pisa in 1347. He joined the Dominicans in 1277, studied at Pisa, Bologna, and Paris, and taught at Lucca, Florence, and Pisa. A renowned preacher, he matched learning with devotion and skill in Latin and Tuscan poetry with mastery of canon and civil law.

His fame rests on the Summa de Casibus Conscientiae, alphabetically arranged and called Pisana, Pisanella, or Bartholomaea. Clear, concise, and current with newer laws, it was hugely popular in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Early printers in Germany, France, and Italy took it up, and Nicholas of Osimo added a supplement in 1444. His De documentis antiquorum, in Tuscan as Ammaestramenti degli antichi, became a Tuscan classic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-of-s:
Benedict of San Philadelphio, also called Benedict the Moor, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Sicily in 1526 to enslaved parents from Ethiopia, he was freed by his parents' master for their faithful service. From youth he lived a devout life and joined a new group of hermits, men who pray apart from the world.

When the pope dissolved that group, Benedict entered the Franciscans, a mendicant order of friars. His virtues raised him to superior of a Palermo monastery, an unusual honour for a lay brother of African birth. The entry presents a humble friar whose holiness outshone the limits his age set for him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardine-a-: Bernardine a Piconio, born Henri Bernardine de Picquigny in Picardy in 1633, died in Paris in 1709. He joined the Capuchins in 1649 and taught theology with distinction. His best-known work, a threefold exposition of St. Paul's letters, appeared at Paris in 1703 and in English in 1706, and stayed popular with Bible scholars, alongside his exposition of the Gospels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardino-te:
Bernardino Telesio, an Italian philosopher who rebelled against Aristotle, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born of a noble family at Cosenza in 1508, he died there in 1588 after study at Milan, Rome, and Padua. At Padua he became a recognised leader of the anti-Aristotelians, thinkers who rejected the Greek master's method and system.

Back in the south, under the patronage of Paul IV, he founded an academy at Cosenza. His chief work, On the Nature of Things According to Their Own Principles, appeared in part at Rome in 1565 and in full at Naples in 1587. The entry presents a bold natural philosopher who urged study of nature itself over books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-besancon-veso:
Besançon, an archdiocese in eastern France, receives a full entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Its land matches the departments of Doubs and Haute-Saône plus the Belfort district, but few dioceses changed shape so often in the nineteenth century. Concordats, Swiss parishes, and the loss of Alsace-Lorraine in 1870 all redrew its map.

Archbishops fill the middle, from Granvelle, minister of Philip II who built the Besançon palace, to Grammont, who fought Jansenism and moved the university from Dôle. Luxeuil, St. Columbanus's monastery, anchors its early fame. The entry is a diocese reshaped by every border war around it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bisarchio: Bisarchio, a Sardinian diocese suffragan to Sassari, takes a short entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Its bishop lives at Ozieri, though early Christian history there is unknown. The first bishop named is Costantino Madrone about 1102, followed by Pietro in 1116. After moves to Giracle and Ardera, and union with Alghero in 1503, Pius VII restored the diocese in 1803.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-henry-of-s:
Blessed Henry of Segusio, usually called Hostiensis, was a thirteenth-century Italian canonist, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Born at Susa, he died at Lyons in 1271 after studying Roman and canon law at Bologna, where he taught and took his doctorate in both laws. Teaching at Paris and a stay in England followed, with a mission from Henry III to Innocent IV.

Provost of Antibes and papal chaplain, he rose to Sisteron in 1244, Embrun in 1250, and Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia in 1262. His Summa on the Decretals became the standard canon-law textbook of the age. The entry presents the greatest canonist of his century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-jacopo-de-:
Blessed Jacopo de Voragine, Archbishop of Genoa and medieval writer of saints' lives, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Viraggio near Genoa about 1230, he died in 1298 after joining the Dominicans in 1244. Fame as a preacher spread through Lombardy, and he taught Scripture and theology before becoming provincial of Lombardy in 1267.

Made Archbishop of Genoa in 1292, he worked to reconcile the city's warring Guelph and Ghibelline factions, with brief success in 1295, and held a synod on the relics of St. Syrus. His Golden Legend, a vast collection of saints' lives, made him the Middle Ages' most-read hagiographer. The entry presents a peacemaker and a storyteller.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brancaccio:
The Brancaccio, an ancient Neapolitan family, gave Naples its Brancacciana Library, state officials, and seven cardinals between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries. Two branches survive today, those of Ruffano and Brancaccio, and France's Brancas descend from the same stock. Their cardinals span schism, councils, and embassies. The family also gave the state many fine servants over the years.

Landolfo, made cardinal in 1294, served Boniface VIII and Clement V and attended Vienne. Luigi, a learned canonist, became Archbishop of Taranto and cardinal in 1408. Nicolo backed antipopes Clement VII and Benedict XIII. Rinaldo and Tommaso attended Constance, Francesco Maria, cardinal in 1634, even debated whether chocolate breaks a fast, and Stefano, cardinal in 1681, served as nuncio at Florence and Venice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cassano-all-i:
Cassano all' Ionio is a diocese suffragan to Reggio, its city in Cosenza province in Calabria, set in a fertile hollow of a steep mountain. Known in Caesar's time as Cassanum, its see has no known founding date, though a bishop appears in 1059 and another, Saxo, in 1096. Its bishops form a long roll. Antonello dei Gesualdi was learned in canon and civil law, and Belforte Spinelli attended Constance as a layman before retiring to Venice.

Later names include Cristoforo Giacoazzi, called to Rome by Paul III for his skill in church affairs, and Giovanni Angelo Medici, afterwards Pius IV. An Englishman, Audoeno Ludovico Cambrone, sent on papal missions, never lived in Cassano. Theatines and Augustinians follow in the list, and the diocese counts 130,000 people in 46 parishes, with 200 churches and chapels and 263 priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comacchio:
Umberto Benigni's entry covers Comacchio, a diocese suffragan of Ravenna. The town lies in Ferrara province in the Romagna, on islands near the mouths of the Po. A canal built by Cardinal Palotta joins it to the sea. Its old name was Cymaclum. Pacatianus, present at a Roman synod in 503 under Pope Symmachus, stands as its first known bishop. Saint Gregory the Great counts the see among Ravenna's suffragans. In the fifteenth century Venice held the town, but Alfonso II of Ferrara retook it in 1509.

At Alfonso's death in 1597, Comacchio passed with Ferrara under the Holy See. Bishop Alfonso Pandolfo, in 1631, wrote polished verse and prose and founded the Accademia dei Fluttuanti. Nearby stands the shrine of Santa Maria in Aula Regia, reached by a portico of 142 arches from 1647. The diocese counted 40,630 people, with 114 parishes, 26 secular and 6 regular priests, and the famed Benedictine Abbey of Pomposa within its bounds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-family-of-ben:
The Bentivoglio were a powerful family of Bologna in medieval Italy. They claimed descent from Enzio, a son of Emperor Frederick II. Rising through the guilds in the fourteenth century, they ruled Bologna in the fifteenth. Their name marks a long run of civic power and patronage.

Cardinal Guido Bentivoglio, born in 1579, served as nuncio in Flanders and France. He also acted as protector of French interests at Rome. Cardinal Cornelio Bentivoglio, born in 1668, served as nuncio in Paris. He later became a minister of Spain and opposed the Jansenists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-federigo-baro:
Federigo Baroccio was a painter and engraver of Urbino, called Fiore d'Urbino. Born in 1528, he learned his first art lessons from his sculptor father. He studied in Rome under Raphael's influence and copied Titian. His subjects were chiefly religious, including many large altarpieces.

Pius IV set him with Zuccaro to decorate the little Vatican palace of Belvedere. Poisoned, it is said, by jealous painters, he never fully recovered. For the rest of his life he worked only a few hours each day. Works by him hang in the Louvre, London, Urbino, and Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felice-anerio:
Felice Anerio was an eminent Roman composer of the late Roman Renaissance. Born about 1560, he sang as a boy soprano in the Papal Choir. He studied music under Nanini and later served as choirmaster at Rome's English College. In 1594 he followed Palestrina as composer to the great Papal Choir in Rome.

His post, created for Palestrina, ended with Anerio's own death. Several of his works long passed for years as Palestrina's own compositions. His music shows originality and fine artistic feeling throughout. Many pieces survive only in manuscript in various Roman libraries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felix-de-lope:
Lope de Vega was the great dramatist of Spain's Golden Age. Born at Madrid in 1562, he wrote his first play at the age of fourteen. He served in the navy and sailed with the Armada against England. By 1600 he ruled the Spanish stage as its acknowledged arbiter.

His output spanned epics, lyrics, pastorals, and an astonishing number of plays. After his second wife's death he became a priest about 1614. Orders did not reform his life, which stayed disordered and worldly to the end. He died in 1635, mourned in a magnificent funeral cortege.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriello-fal:
Gabriello Fallopio, an anatomist born at Modena in 1523, left his name on the tube that bears the egg from ovary to womb. Poor but noble-born, he fought his way to a medical degree at Ferrara. He taught anatomy there in 1548, moved to Pisa, and in 1551 took the anatomy chair at Padua under Cosimo I. He died there in 1562, not yet forty.

Fallopio's chief work lay in the head: the inner ear, the eardrum and its bony ring, the round and oval windows, and the link between mastoid cells and middle ear. He mapped tear passages and the ethmoid bone, corrected Vesalius on muscles, and first used an ear speculum in practice. His canal for the facial nerve, the aqueduct of Fallopio, joins the tube in keeping his name alive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giorgio-clovi:
Giorgio Clovio, also known as Giulio Clovio, was a famous Italian miniaturist born at Grizani on the Croatian coast in 1498, who died at Rome in 1578. Vasari called him the unique and the little Michelangelo. Coming to Italy at eighteen, he won renown and became a protégé of Cardinal Grimani. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a career spent painting tiny masterpieces for popes and princes.

After a vow made when bandits seized him in 1527, he took orders at Mantua and took the name Giulio in religion. Released from his vows, he painted a Latin missal, a Petrarch, and, for Cardinal Farnese, a prayer book Vasari called a divine work. Philip II and John III of Portugal also paid handsomely for his work. Yet his grand Renaissance manner, the article argues, helped crowd out the older, daintier art of miniature painting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-bocc:
Giovanni Boccaccio was an Italian novelist born in Paris in 1313, who died at Certaldo in 1375. His father, a merchant from Certaldo, brought the boy to Florence, put him to school, and sent him to Naples in 1327 to study law. There he gave himself to literature and the court of Anjou. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows him from law student to public man and friend of Petrarch.

After 1350 his friendship with Petrarch lasted until the latter's death in 1374. In 1373, despite age and Florence's political strife, he began lecturing on Dante's poems. His early works include the Filocolo, a version of Floire and Blanchefleur, and the Teseide, whose tale of Palamon and Arcite Chaucer used for his Knight's Tale. The Fiammetta, among his best-written books, draws on his love for Maria d'Acquino.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-fran:
Giovanni Francesco Anerio was a composer born at Rome about 1567, who died about 1620. For four years he sang as a chorister at St. Peter's under Palestrina. He served as choirmaster to Sigismund III of Poland in 1609 and at Verona cathedral in 1610, then taught music at the Seminario Romano. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a musician of the old and new styles together.

From 1613 to 1620 he led the choir at Santa Maria de' Monti, taking holy orders in 1616. Among the first Italian composers to use the quaver and its subdivisions, he left a large body of sacred music. His collections bore fanciful titles like Ghirlanda di Sacre Rose and Selva armonica. He also reset Palestrina's Missa Papae Marcelli for four voices, making the six-voice mass more practicable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-stef:
Giovanni Stefano Menochio was a Jesuit biblical scholar born at Padua in 1575, who died at Rome in 1655. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1594, taught classics, then became professor of sacred scripture and of moral theology at Milan. He rose through posts as superior of Cremona, Milan, and Genoa. He served as rector of the Roman College and provincial of Milan and Rome. A Catholic Encyclopedia article praises a commentator still famous for clarity.

His first exegetical essay was a 956-page study of politics drawn from scripture, Hieropoliticon of 1625, followed by an economic study of the Bible in 1627. His lasting work, the three-volume Brevis Explicatio of the literal sense of scripture, went through many editions across Europe. Friends and foes praised his brevity and critical judgment, and his notes entered the great biblical collections of de La Haye and Migne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giulio-alenio:
Giulio Alenio was a Chinese missionary and scholar born at Brescia in Italy in 1582, who died at Fou-Tcheou in China in August 1644. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1600, already noted for mathematics and theology. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a Jesuit who wrote widely in Chinese.

Sent to China in 1610, he waited at Macao for a chance to enter the country. He published there his result of the lunar eclipse of 8 November 1612. Once inside China he preached in the provinces of Xan-si and Fi-Kien. His many Chinese works include a controversial treatise against Chinese errors, The True Origin of All Things, and a life of God the Saviour drawn from the Four Gospels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giulio-lorenz:
Giulio Lorenzo Selvaggio was a canonist and archaeologist born at Naples on 10 August 1728, who died there in November 1772. In 1744 he entered the Naples seminary, and in 1752 he was ordained priest. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a scholar cut off before finishing his chief work.

He gave himself to history, philosophy, and the Oriental languages. He served as censor of books and synodal examiner for Naples, and wrote notes for the Italian edition of Mosheim's ecclesiastical history. Made professor of canon law in 1764, he published Institutionum canonicarum libri tres at Padua in 1770. He set out to treat Christian antiquities in a smaller work after Mamachi's unfinished one, but died before finishing it, and his friend Kalephati continued the publication.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gubbio:
Umbria's Gubbio, ancient Iguvium, is known first for the Gubbio Tables, seven bronze slabs with inscriptions in Latin and the old Umbrian tongue. Found in 1444, they were set into the town hall walls. The find gave the first push to the study of ancient Italian dialects. The entry moves from that treasure through Roman conquest in 49 BC to a populous medieval commune.

St. Ubaldo, bishop of the city, directed its famous 1151 victory over Perugia and ten other towns, and later lords included the Gabrielli and the Montefeltro dukes of Urbino. Bishops run from Decentius, addressed by Innocent I in 416, to Marcello Cervino, later Pope Marcellus II. The see closes with 65 parishes and 40,200 souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guglielmo-aud:
Guglielmo Audisio, born at Bra in Piedmont in 1801 and dead in Rome in 1882, taught sacred eloquence at Bra's seminary. He headed Turin's Academy of Superga until Piedmont's anti-clerical politics cost him the post. Pius IX then made him professor of natural and popular rights at the Roman University and a canon of the Vatican Basilica.

Audisio spent freely on charity and his manual of sacred eloquence travelled in many languages. His histories of the papacy, though industrious, lost value as new documents appeared. Accused of Gallicanism at the Vatican Council, he grieved, submitted fully when his book on political and religious society was condemned in 1877, and had helped found Turin's intransigent Catholic paper Armonia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guido-de-bays:
Guido de Baysio, an Italian canon lawyer born about the middle of the thirteenth century, earned lasting fame under the name Archidiaconus. A noble Ghibelline from Reggio who studied under Guido de Suzaria, he taught canon law at Bologna. He became its archdeacon and university chancellor under Boniface VIII in 1296, and ended his career at Avignon in the papal chancery.

His chief work, the Rosarium of about 1300, gathers older glosses on Gratian's Decretum that the standard Glossa Ordinaria had left out, chiefly from Huguccio, and later editions drew on it heavily. At Avignon he also wrote a full commentary on the Liber Sextus and a tract defending Boniface VIII that grew out of the Templars' trial at Vienne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hamilton-onta:
Ontario's Diocese of Hamilton, suffragan of Toronto, was cut from Toronto by bull in February 1856 and covers eight counties with 55,000 people, 42 churches, and 61 priests. Its first bishop, Irish-born John Farrell, consecrated in May 1856, brought Catholic schools, built St. Mary's cathedral, and set up Loretto academies at Hamilton and Guelph.

Successors Crinnon and Carbery added churches, a House of Providence, and a diocesan synod. Bishop Dowling, installed in 1889, founded fourteen parishes, ordained twenty-eight priests, and raised hospitals at Hamilton and Guelph. Fifty-one separate schools teach 6,000 pupils under Sisters of St. Joseph, Loretto, and Notre Dame, and the cathedral was consecrated in May 1906 for the diocesan golden jubilee.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-huguccio:
Huguccio, also called Hugh of Pisa, was an Italian canonist, born at Pisa at an unknown date and dead in 1210. Bologna, probably under Gandolphus, saw his studies, and there he taught canon law, perhaps in the school attached to the monastery of Sts. Nabor and Felix. Ferrara gained him as bishop in 1190.

Lothario de' Conti, later Innocent III, numbered among his pupils. He held Huguccio in high esteem and sent important cases to him, traces of which remain in canon law collections. Two letters from Innocent III to Huguccio entered Gregory IX's Decretals. Besides a book on etymologies, Huguccio wrote a Summa on Gratian's Decretum. It was finished in 1187 or after 1190. It ranked as the most extensive and perhaps most authoritative commentary of its time, though it skips four causes later filled by Joannes de Deo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-internuncio:
A papal diplomat below the five highest ranks yet still chief of a legation is the figure defined here. From Latin words for between and messenger, the internuncio heads a mission, sometimes with several staff and sometimes with only a private secretary. No fixed rule governs his posting. Internuncios have served countries of widely different church importance, from Luxemburg and Holland to Chile and Brazil.

In older days slow post and no telegraph forced wide powers on such envoys, since they could not wait for Rome's word. Modern communications have shrunk their role to routine business, though grave affairs can still bring extraordinary powers. The entry gives a small but exact portrait of a rank in the papal diplomatic ladder that most readers never meet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jonas-of-bobb:
Jonas of Bobbio, or Jonas of Susa, was a seventh-century monk and hagiographer of St. Columbanus. Born near the close of the sixth century at Susa in Piedmont, he entered Bobbio in 618 and became secretary to Abbots Attala and Bertulf. He accompanied the latter to Rome in 628 before settling permanently in Gaul.

Called by St. Amandus to help mission work among the heathen of Belgium and northern France, he wrote the life of St. Vaast, first Frankish Bishop of Arras. Promising Bobbio's monks during a visit in 639, he wrote between 640 and 643 his chief work, the Life of St. Columbanus, with lives of Attala, Bertulf, Eustace of Luxeuil, and Abbess Fara. Arriving at Bobbio only three years after Columbanus's death, he drew on men who had known the saint, and Bede wove his lives into English church history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-caballer:
Juan Caballero y Ocio was a Mexican priest famed for lavish charity in Querétaro. Born there in 1644, he served as mayor while still a layman, then took orders and held high church offices. He gave large sums to churches, founded and endowed the Jesuit church and college in his city, and built Dominican, Capuchin, and Loretto foundations.

Caballero gave dowries to over two hundred girls, built a hospital, and gave 150,000 dollars to the new California missions. He refused two bishoprics and the title of governor of California. Each year he made a retreat and redrew his will, acting as executor of his own gifts. His bequests grew for a century and a half until Mexico's spoliation of the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-legio:
Legio was a titular see of Palestina Secunda, suffragan of Scythopolis, appearing first in a Latin episcopal notitia probably from the eleventh century, listed as Legionum between Diocaesarea and Capitolias. The Greek Notitiae, whose Latin version is only a translation, give not Legio but Maximianopolis in that place.

Legio's see is therefore the same place as Maximianopolis. In the Middle Ages the two cities were identified, being near neighbours, though they were truly distinct places within one see. Legio is now Ledjun, famous in Bible and history under the name Mageddo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-london-ontari:
London, Ontario, is a Canadian diocese set up in 1855, covering nine counties in south-west Ontario. The city of London itself, then about ten thousand strong with a fifth Catholic, became the see the next year.

Pierre-Adolphe Pinsonnault, a Sulpician from Quebec, served as first bishop, then moved the seat to Sandwich in 1859. John Walsh brought it back to London in 1869, began a new cathedral in 1881, and later rose to Toronto. Denis O'Connor followed him to Toronto in 1899, and Fergus Patrick McEvay took the London see that same year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenzo-campe:
Lorenzo Campeggio was a cardinal, canon lawyer, diplomat, and reformer, born at Bologna in 1472 or 1474 and dead at Rome in 1539. Son of a famed civil lawyer, he studied law at Padua and Bologna, married, raised five children, and entered church life after his wife died in 1509.

Julius II made him Bishop of Feltre in 1512 and a judge of the Rota, the Church's high court. As legate he worked in Germany and England through the Reformation's first storms, sharing power with Wolsey in London and holding Salisbury until 1534. Later missions took him to Hungary, Poland, and the German diets, where he pressed for reform and for war against the Turks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-buglio:
Louis Buglio was a Jesuit missionary, mathematician, and theologian in China, born in Sicily in 1606 and dead at Peking in 1682. After teaching humanities and rhetoric at the Roman College, he asked for the Chinese mission and preached with zeal in Szechwan, Fukien, and Kiangsi.

Captured in persecution under the young Kangxi emperor, he was taken to Peking in 1648 and soon left free to minister. With Schall, Verbiest, and Magalhaens he helped reform the Chinese calendar and won the emperor's trust. Fluent in Chinese, he wrote over eighty volumes and translated the Missal, Breviary, and Ritual for native priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luca-marenzio:
Luca Marenzio was an Italian composer, born near Brescia in 1550 and dead at Rome in 1599. His chief gift to music lies in his books of madrigals, short part-songs for voices, of which he left 159 madrigals and motets.

His first book appeared in 1581, dedicated to Alfonso d'Este of Ferrara, and Musica Transalpina carried his pieces to England in 1588, where they caught on at once. An eight-part Mass ranks with the great church masses, and his Villanelle e Arie alla Napolitana holds 113 dainty pieces for three and four voices. Proske's modern editions in Musica Divina keep his finest work in print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ludovico-bert:
Ludovico Bertonio was an Italian Jesuit missionary and linguist of the Aymara tongue, born near Ancona in 1552 and dead at Lima in 1625. He joined the Society in 1575 and sailed to Peru six years later, working chiefly among Aymara Indians of southern Peru and Bolivia.

His grammars and vocabularies, printed at Rome in 1603 and at the Jesuit press at Juli in 1612, gave Europe its first solid grip on Aymara. A short grammar, a full grammar, a two-part vocabulary, a bilingual confessional, and a life of Christ in Aymara and Spanish all came from his pen. Later scholars reprinted his rare books in facsimile and cleared him of inventing the name Aymara.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maffeo-vegio:
Maffeo Vegio, Mapheus Vegius, was a churchman, humanist, poet, and educator, born at Lodi in 1406 and dead at Rome in 1458. Raised at Lodi and Milan under teachers who took pupils to hear Bernardine of Siena, whose life he later wrote, he studied at Pavia. He moved from philosophy to law, then to letters, devoted above all to Virgil.

He published poems at sixteen, taught poetry and law at Pavia for about ten years, and championed the revival of letters. Eugenius IV made him secretary of papal briefs, then apostolic datary and canon of St. Peter's, and his studies turned from Virgil to Augustine, drawing him into the Augustinian order. His fame rests on his supplement to the Aeneid, tracing Aeneas's destiny, beside poems on the Golden Fleece, Astyanax, and St. Anthony.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manius-aciliu:
Manius Acilius Glabrio was consul at Rome in A.D. 91, alongside Trajan. He came from one of Rome's noblest houses. Nine men of his name had held the consulship. The first, consul in 191 B.C., beat the Macedonians at Thermopylae. Family gardens in the early empire covered what is now the Pincian Hill.

Domitian had Glabrio put to death in 95, after banishing him. Suetonius says the emperor killed senators and ex-consuls as contrivers of novelty. In Glabrio's case that charge seems to mean Christian faith. Dio Cassius adds that Domitian forced him, during his consulship, to fight a lion and two bears at Albanum. His body reached Rome and lay in the Priscilla catacomb on the Via Salaria. Its crypt, found in 1888, held a sarcophagus inscribed to Acilius Glabrio, proof of his family burial and, with the Domitian-era lettering, of his martyrdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mario-di-cala:
Mario di Calasio was a Friar Minor and lexicographer, born at Calasio in Naples about 1550 and dead at Rome in 1620. He joined the Franciscans and mastered Hebrew so well that the pope called him to Rome. There he taught Hebrew at Ara Coeli and San Pietro in Montorio.

Paul V favoured him, made him his confessor, and gave him the titles and privileges of doctors of theology. Dying, he had the Passion read to him and passed away chanting David's Psalms in Hebrew. His fame rests chiefly on the Concordantiae Sacrorum Bibliorum Hebraicorum, published at Rome in 1622, two years after his death. A lesser London edition followed in 1747. He also wrote a Hebrew dictionary and general canons of the holy tongue, grounding his name in Semitic scholarship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-anton-:
Martin Anton Delrio was a scholar, statesman, and Jesuit theologian, born at Antwerp in 1551 and dead at Louvain in 1608. He studied at Paris, Douai, Louvain, and Salamanca, taking a law doctorate in 1574. 

He joined the Jesuits in 1580, made novitiate at Valladolid, and taught philosophy, moral theology, and Scripture at Douai, Liege, Louvain, Graz, and Salamanca. He spoke at least nine languages, wrote pure if diffuse prose, and prepared books with extreme care: his second work, at twenty-three, cites near eleven hundred authors. His output ranged from commentaries on Claudius, Seneca, Genesis, and the Canticle to a Belgian history, anti-Scaliger pamphlets, and sacred proverb lore. Best known is his six-volume treatise on magic, Disquisitionum magicarum, praised in its day through many editions but no longer fully acceptable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-masaccio:
Masaccio, properly Tommaso di ser Giovanni di Simone dei Guidi, was an Italian painter born about 1402 at San Giovanni di Valdarno and dead probably at Rome in 1429. 

His master was Masolino da Panicale, Little Tom, and at nineteen he already belonged to the Speziali guild, which included painters. After early essays won some fame, he was charged about 1424 or 1426, aged at most twenty-four, with continuing the Brancacci Chapel decoration his master had begun. Many works are lost, but his Santa Maria Novella Trinity, with donors kneeling beside Virgin and St John, survives much damaged, and Florence Academy holds his St Anne with Madonna and Child. Moderately esteemed in life, he won enthusiastic admiration only after death, an enthusiasm five centuries have not cooled. His insight into nature, scientific perspective, and foreshortening won loud and just acclaim.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-motu-proprio:
A motu proprio is a papal rescript named for its clause motu proprio, of his own accord. The clause signals that the pope decided its provisions personally, not on the advice of cardinals or others, but for reasons he himself judged sufficient. In form it resembles a Brief more than a Bull, yet it is neither sealed nor countersigned. It issues from the Dataria Apostolica, and is usually written in Italian or Latin.

It opens with the reason moving the pope, then states the law, regulation or favour granted. It bears his personal signature with name and date in Latin. First issued by Innocent VIII in 1484, it always rankled in France as an infringement of Gallican liberties. The best known recent example is Pius X's 1903 instructions reforming church music.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nuncio:
A nuncio is the pope's ordinary, permanent representative to a sovereign's court or a fixed territory, holding both diplomatic and church powers. Unlike a legate sent for one affair, a nuncio resides in his nunciature, covers all Holy See interests there, and is replaced by a successor when recalled.

The office grew slowly rather than by one decree, from Byzantine apocrisarii through medieval legates to the permanent envoys of the sixteenth century. The entry traces nunciatures country by country, their courts, faculties, and quarrels with kings over jurisdiction and precedence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ohio:
Ohio, admitted to the Union on 19 February 1803 as the seventeenth state, spreads an undulating plain between Lake Erie and the Ohio River. Bounded by Michigan, Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Kentucky, and Indiana, it covers 41,060 square miles and held 4,767,121 people in 1910.

La Salle explored it about 1670, France claimed it in 1671, Britain won it in 1763, and the Ohio Company opened settlement after 1787. Farms, mines, and factories valued near a billion dollars in 1908 anchor the entry, with railroads, canals, and Catholic dioceses mapped beside them. Its railroad mileage reached 9,274 miles, besides 4,450 miles of electric railway.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-onofrio-panvi:
Veronese historian Onofrio Panvinio, born in 1530, became a leading church historian of the Renaissance. Joining the Augustinian Hermits at eleven, he took his first degree at Rome in 1553 and taught theology at Florence. He took his doctor’s degree in 1557 and worked in libraries across Italy and Germany.

He turned down a bishopric and served as corrector of Vatican Library books and died at Palermo in 1568 while attending Cardinal Farnese to Monreale's synod. Manutius called him a devourer of antiquity, Scaliger father of all history, and his Fasti and works on Roman assemblies remain landmarks. His Fasti et Triumphi Romanorum appeared at Venice in 1557, from Romulus to Charles V.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ontario:
Ontario, Canada's most populous and wealthy province, covers 140 million acres besides the Great Lakes, with old settled lands in the south and sparse new lands in the north. Bounded by Quebec, James Bay, Manitoba, Minnesota, and four great lakes, it holds extremes of climate softened by dry inland air.

France held it until 1763, Champlain visited in 1615, and Jesuits Brébeuf and Lalemant died as martyrs in 1649 amid Indian wars. The entry follows settlement, railroads, mines, and farms, with Catholic dioceses, schools, and parishes from Ottawa to the northern missions. Old Ontario lies settled between the Ottawa, Saint Lawrence, and the Great Lakes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oratorio:
An oratorio, as now understood, sets a religious text, usually from Scripture, for solo voices, chorus, orchestra, and organ, with drama carried by music alone. Tradition ties its birth to Philip Neri's oratory, though critics note his chapels suited no sacred drama.

The answer lies in Cavalieri's Anima e Corpo, performed at the Vallicella in 1600, five years after Philip's death, with the name oratorio arriving sixty years later. From madrigal roots and liturgical polyphony, the form grew through Carissimi, Handel, and Haydn into the modern concert sacred drama. Only after six decades did the label oratorio attach to the new form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palma-vecchio:
Palma Vecchio, born Jacopo Nigreti at Serinalta near Bergamo about 1480 and dead at Venice on 30 July 1528, studied under Giovanni Bellini beside Giorgione and Lotto. From Bellini he took the model for his altarpieces, adding freer arrangement. His works run strong and broad rather than graceful, and following Giorgione he treated sacred themes as genre scenes, full of vigour, life, and clear colour, though short on religious feeling.

His favourite theme was the Holy Conversation, the Holy Family or Madonna ringed by saints, seen at Rome, Florence, Dresden, Munich, and Vienna. Among his pieces stand a Madonna with Saints George and Lucy, an Adoration of the Shepherds in the Louvre, and a Meeting of Jacob and Rachel at Dresden. His master work, a triptych of Saint Barbara between Anthony the Hermit and Saint Sebastian, hangs at Santa Maria Formosa in Venice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piatto-cardin:
The piatto cardinalizio was the pope's allowance to cardinals serving in Rome or employed by the Church, letting them keep their dignity with decorum. Cardinals maintained in Rome by their sovereigns received none, and nobly born cardinals declined it. A cardinal with other income got only enough to top up his revenues to the allowance.

The name dates from the conclave of 1458. Paul II set the poor cardinal's plate at 100 gold florins a month for revenues under 4,000 florins. Paul V raised it to 1,500 scudi a year. Custom then gave 6,000 scudi to cardinals without church income, and 1746 cut it to 4,000 scudi, the figure still standing, with benefices renounced. Distinguished cardinals sometimes drew more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-metast:
Pietro Metastasio was the Italian poet whose opera librettos, words set to music, delighted Europe in the eighteenth century. He was born at Rome in 1698 as Trapassi, the son of a former papal soldier turned pork-butcher. He was taken up by the scholar Vincenzo Gravina, who gave him a classical education and a Hellenised pen name.

After early success with the musical drama Orti Esperidi at Naples, he became imperial poet at Vienna in 1730 on the recommendation of Apostolo Zeno. In the next decade he wrote more than seventy melodramas, among them Didone, Artaserse, and his masterpiece Attilio Regolo. He won crowds with clear dialogue, homely wisdom, and tunes that pleased ordinary listeners.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pinar-del-rio:
Pinar del Río is a Cuban diocese covering the western end of the island. It was erected by Pope Leo XIII in February 1903 and matches the civil province in bounds. It spans 2,867 square miles and holds twenty-seven parishes served by nineteen secular priests, clergy not bound to a religious order.

Its first bishop, Braulio de Orne y Vivanco, was consecrated at Havana in October 1903 and died the next year. He was succeeded by Manuel Ruiz y Rodríguez, consecrated at Cienfuegos in 1907. The entry also notes a boys' school run by the Piarist Fathers and a girls' school in the care of religious sisters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pinturicchio:
Pinturicchio, born Bernardino di Betto at Perugia about 1454, was an Italian fresco painter nicknamed the dauber for his quick facility. He trained under Fiorenzo di Lorenzo and assisted Perugino in the Sistine Chapel in 1480. Two frescoes there, the Baptism of Jesus and Moses journeying to Egypt, are now recognised as his.

His chief work was the Borgia Apartment in the Vatican, painted for Alexander VI. Its Hall of Saints, with graceful histories of martyrs such as Susanna, Barbara, and Sebastian, is the finest room. He enlivened his frescoes with gilded relief in the Sienese manner, painted the chapel at Spello with Sibyls and scenes of Christ's childhood, and died at Siena in 1513.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-antonio:
San Antonio, a Texas diocese between the Colorado and Rio Grande rivers, covers about 90,909 square miles, excepting land south of the Arroyo de los Hermanos and four coastal counties. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia opens with French priests, not Spaniards, as the first ministers of the region. La Salle's expedition entered Matagorda Bay in January 1685 and built Fort St Louis.

Five priests laboured two years in the fort chapel, Franciscans Membré, Le Clercq, and Douay with Sulpicians Chefdeville and Cavelier, before abandoning Texas for Canada. Franciscans from Querétaro and Zacatecas then founded missions on the Rio Grande. The entry follows Spanish mission work through the eighteenth century to the modern diocese, with its parishes, schools, and bishops serving a vast border land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-no:
The Cleveland branch of the Sisters of Notre Dame grew from the congregation founded by Julie Billiart. In 1850 Father Elting of Coesfeld, Germany, brought the order into Westphalia with Hildegonda Wollbring and Lisette Kuehling as first members. Novices trained under three sisters from the mother-house, and the branch grew into a teaching community.

After the teaching sisters were expelled, Father Westerholt of Saint Peter's Church, Cleveland, had Bishop Gilmour invite them to Ohio. On 5 July 1874 the superior general arrived in New York with eight sisters, reaching Cleveland the next day. They took charge of a parish school for girls within two months, and later conducted more than forty parish schools in Ohio and Kentucky, with about 14,000 pupils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-berard-of-:
St. Berard of Carbio, or Beraldus, was a Friar Minor and martyr, dead on 16 January 1220. This entry follows a man of the noble Leopardi family, a native of Carbio in Umbria, received into the Franciscan order by Francis himself in 1213. He was well versed in Arabic and an eloquent preacher. Francis chose him, with two other priests, Peter and Otho, and two lay brothers, Accursius and Adjutus, to evangelize the unbelievers of the East.

On the conclusion of the Second General Chapter in 1219, Francis believed the time had come for his order to extend its apostolic labours beyond the Italian peninsula and northern Europe. For himself and twelve others he chose the greater part of Syria and Egypt, giving Berard and his companions the Moroccan missions. The five set sail from Italy, and after some time in Spain and Portugal, they arrived in the kingdom of Morocco.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-braulio:
St. Braulio was bishop of Saragossa, date of birth unknown, dead at Saragossa about 651. This entry follows a man who in 631 succeeded his brother John, whose archdeacon he had been, in the Saragossa see. His influence reached bishops and the kings of Spain alike. In one letter he pressed King Chindaswinth to name his son Receswinth co-regent.

His insistence with his friend Isidore of Seville brought the latter's Libri Etymologiarum to inception and completion. Braulio attended the Toledo synods of 633, 636, and 638. The last council selected him to answer Pope Honorius I, who had reproached the Spanish bishops with negligence in pastoral duties. In his letter Braulio cleverly and fearlessly defended the Spanish episcopate, and towards the end of his life he complained bitterly of losing his eyesight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-toledo-ohio:
Toledo, Ohio, is a diocese formed from Cleveland and erected on 15 April 1910. It covers sixteen counties in northwest Ohio, an area of 6,969 square miles, with Lima, Tiffin, Fremont, Defiance and Delphos among its towns. Its Catholic population was estimated at 125,000, served by eighty-six parishes with resident priests and twenty-five missions.

Ninety-five diocesan priests and thirty-one regular clergy staffed the diocese, with sixty-five parish schools enrolling 13,500 pupils, a Jesuit college and three academy-colleges. Charity work ran through three orphanages, two hospitals, a home for the aged poor and a house of the Good Shepherd. The entry also traces the region's French missionary past, from Detroit and the Maumee fort of 1680 to the bishops who pressed for the new see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-urbs-beata-je:
Urbs beata Jerusalem, dicta pacis visio is the first line of a hymn probably from the seventh or eighth century, in eight stanzas plus a doxology.
